Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian Special educational needs Pupils with Send plans in England likely to double to one in 10 in rush for support Schools and councils express financial concerns as EHCP applications surge before potential change in provision ‘Powerful example’: minister looks to Essex school for blueprint to transform Send provision Richard Adams Education editor Sun 6 Sep 2026 12.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 15.55 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Schools and councils across England are expecting the proportion of children with special needs plans to double to one in 10, with families rushing to secure support before ministers bring in changes. Headteachers have reported an “unreal” surge in applications for education, health and care plans (EHCPs) mandating support for needs or disabilities such as speech and learning difficulties, autism or ADHD. In 2025, just one in 20 school-age children had EHCPs. The number of pupils with EHCPs has risen by more than 11% in each of the past two years, and projections by local authorities seen by the Guardian are anticipating similar double-digit annual increases over the next three years. Similar levels nationally would mean just under 10% of all school-age children with an EHCP in 2029. Such a rapid increase would outstrip the government’s own forecasts and eat into funding for improving specialist support in mainstream schools, undermining its plans for immediate reform while straining school and council budgets. School leaders said their special educational needs (Send) coordinators had worked through the summer to deal with the influx of requests for assessments, as secondary schools say that many more year 7 pupils are arriving with EHCPs or applications. One described the volume of requests as “unreal”, while other schools said they expected to have double the number of incoming pupils with EHCPs when the new academic year begins this month. Some parents of special school pupils in England spending £5,000 on EHCPs Read more Bill Revans, the County Councils Network’s spokesperson on special educational needs and disabilities (Send), and the Liberal Democrat leader of Somerset council, said: “It is clear there has been a particularly sharp surge in assessment requests to our member councils this year since the government announced its planned reforms in February. “Our previous analysis had predicted the number of EHCPs will rise to 840,000 by 2028-29, however, it is now likely these numbers will be exceeded. “This translates to very real financial pressures on local authorities, and despite the government commitment to wipe 90% of existing Send deficits built up by councils over the past decade, we expect the debt to be re-accrued by as soon as this time next year.” EHCPs are legal documents agreed between local authorities and families in England detailing the support required for children and young people up to the age of 25, allowing access to extra funding or places in special schools. While more than 530,000 school-age children have EHCPs, an additional 1.3 million have identified special needs , according to official data . The costs are met out of local authority high needs budgets but the massive growth in EHCPs has led to councils amassing sustained deficits, and require a statutory override granted by central government to avoid many local authorities becoming technically bankrupt . Georgia Gould, the schools minister overseeing the changes, said the government was carefully considering the responses to its white paper , which aims to give children earlier diagnosis and intervention and moderate the need for EHCPs. The white paper’s timeline would mean more children get individual support plans alongside increased support in mainstream schools; while EHCPs would be designed for those with more profound needs and disabilities from 2030. During a visit to Thomas Lord Audley secondary school in Colchester, Gould said parts of the planned changes would begin operating this year, including the government’s new “experts in hand” scheme that puts specialists directly into mainstream schools and nurseries. “I’ve spoken to parents around the country, and lots of families and children have been really let down by the system,” Gould said. “So they are really concerned, and any change can feel worrying for those families. View image in fullscreen Georgia Gould, the schools minister, on a visit to a school in Colchester, said she families have been let down by the system. Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian “That’s why we want to put in place tangible change they can see and feel in classrooms and in their communities. And we’ve been clear that we will build a new and inclusive system before we bring in wider changes. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion “We’re really determined to put that support in place so parents don’t need to fight, the support will be readily available at their school, and so no child falls through the cracks.” Gould acknowledged that it was “going to take time to build that trust, to work with families for them to see that day to day. All the work we are doing, the investment, the teacher training, the sharing of best practice, is so important.” Paul Whiteman, the general secretary of the National Association of Head Teachers, said the reports of increases in EHCPs chimed with “what we hear from school leaders”. Whiteman said: “While it is hard to give a definitive reason for why this is happening, it appears likely that the government’s plans to restrict future EHCPs to children with the most complex needs may have led to more families and schools applying before these changes kick-in.” Send plan for England gets cautious welcome amid workload concerns Read more Ipsea, a charity that helps families navigate the special needs system, said its helplines had received most calls about EHCP provision since March, after the changes were announced. Madeleine Cassidy, Ipsea ’s chief executive, said: “The government’s proposed Send reforms risk making an already fragile system worse by removing the statutory protections and vital safeguards available to children and families when support is delayed, denied or inadequate.” The surge in applications has led some local authorities to dramatically raise their own forecasts. A report by Hampshire council in July showed applications so far this year were at record levels and forecasted a 58% increase in EHCPs between 2026 and 2030. Manchester council is also anticipating a 40% increase in school-age children with EHCPs by 2029. William Burns, a social care policy adviser for the Chartered Institute of Public Finance and Accountancy, said a forthcoming survey of local authority treasurers was likely to reveal that the renewed push for EHCPs was creating financial pressures. Burns said: “The government’s own modelling suggests demand for EHCPs could return to today’s levels by 2035, yet current levels of demand are already placing severe strain on the system. It is therefore difficult to see how recreating today’s volume of need, even within a reformed framework, can be considered a sustainable end state.” Explore more on these topics Special educational needs Schools School funding Local government Children Education policy England news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Education Schools Teachers Universities Students

https://nineoclock.ro/luca-niculescu-int.text: ABOUT US NINE O’CLOCK STAFF 2024 COMMERCIAL OFFER – 2026 Subscribe to the Nine O’Clock 2026 CONTACT Special price offer 2026 with a 50% discount Luca Niculescu Interview with Nine O’Clock: Romania’s OECD Accession and Foreign Policy Priorities — State Secretary at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs Originally published on May 28, 2024. Republished online In this interview, Nine O’Clock had the pleasure of speaking with Mr. Niculescu about the governance challenges facing Romania, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs’ role in meeting international standards, and the expected impact of OECD membership on domestic governance. Nine O’Clock : What are the main governance challenges Romania faces in its OECD accession process, and how do you plan to address them? Luca Niculescu : Currently, 26 technical Committees are reviewing Romania’s legislation, policies and practices against OECD standards, best policies and practices in a wide array of areas, covering almost every area of government policy. The reviews are evidence-based following in-depth information-gathering and analysis, including questionnaires and fact-finding missions. Since we have started the Committee review process last year, a considerable number of reviews have taken place in autumn 2023 and in spring 2024. This resulted in the adoption of several technical opinions and one Formal Opinion. The review process will progress further significantly this year, with more than 20 reviews tabled before various OECD Committees. In terms of challenges, these are mainly related to the recommendations resulting from the in-depth assessment by OECD technical Committees. One such example is the Economic Survey of Romania, recently launched in March 2024, which offers a comprehensive review of Romania’s economy and public policies and serves as a key tool in the accession process, as well as a medium-to-long term compass. The Economic Survey includes recommendations as well, which are taken very seriously given that, besides supporting our greater alignment with OECD best policies and practices, they are also linked to our governmental objectives in terms of increasing resilience and recovery. Some of these recommendations to improve public policies in priority areas aim at: completing the fiscal and pensions reform, improving the business environment (e.g. by enforcing and monitoring updated corporate governance framework, improving access to finance and continuing to cover gaps in the fight against corruption), as well as providing adequate conditions and measures that allow the economy to adapt to the green and digital transitions. This is a collaborative process, in which the Committees and the OECD Secretariat are providing support on delivering in this regard. We are also looking at the experience of other countries that recently underwent the accession process and at the areas that required the most effort on their part. Generally, issues such as market openness on an equal level for all OECD Member States, the liberalisation of capital movements, corporate governance of state-owned enterprises, environmental policies, public governance, taxation policies, and combating bribery are challenging for all candidate countries. To sum up, the accession process can serve as a powerful catalyst for important reforms and effectively support the domestic policy agenda. There is therefore the possibility to improve the lives of citizens, in line with the OECD motto better policies for better lives . Nine O’Clock : How does the Ministry of Foreign Affairs contribute to shaping Romania’s governance practices to meet international standards? Luca Niculescu : : By virtue of its role as national coordinator of the OECD accession process, the MFA, supported by the General Secretariat and the Chancellery of the Government, oversees the entire process, ensures the continued engagement and commitment of all Romanian national authorities, and promotes good understanding of the different phases in the process. We facilitate the dialogue at both technical and political-diplomatic level between the OECD Secretariat and OECD Member States and our national authorities across public policies within the entire socio-economic spectrum and assist them in moving towards the implementation of the recommendations. Our role is also to make sure that we stay the course, we keep the rhythm and continue to advance smoothly within the accession process. On a different note, the accession process serves also to confirm Romania’s adherence to the values, vision and priorities of the OECD. As a like-minded community, OECD Members commit to certain values that accession candidate countries are expected to share, in particular on: the preservation of individual liberty; the values of democracy, the rule of law and the protection of human rights; and the value of open, trading, competitive, sustainable and transparent market economies. The MFA plays an important role in this regard by actively engaging in multilateral fora in defending shared values with like-minded countries unified by the commitment to a rules-based international order. In terms of public governance, within the OECD’s Directorate for Public Governance, a Public Governance Committee (PGC) focuses on proposing strategic, evidence-based and innovative policies for strengthening the capacity of governments to respond to citizen’s needs and help governments address economic, social and environmental challenges effectively. The Committee plays a key role in shaping public governance policies and strategies covering a wide array of areas spanning from public procurement and access to justice to digitalization of public services and combating disinformation. Romania had a very good first accession review by the Public Governance Committee in April this year, which acknowledged the important progress achieved thus far. Over the past years the General Secretariat of the Government and other institutions worked together with the OECD Secretariat on instrumental projects, such as Reviews on Open Government, Civic Space, Digital Government, Innovation in Public Sector, Public integrity. These helped us in achieving several milestones in improving our policies in public governance. Nine O’Clock : How do you anticipate Romania’s integration into global governance frameworks like the OECD will affect its domestic governance? Luca Niculescu : : The Romanian Government is consistently committed to achieving full alignment with OECD standards and practices. There is a solid cross-party political commitment by Romania to continue its efforts to implement all the necessary changes. Moreover, in facing ongoing geo-strategic and geo-economic challenges, we must continue to come up with collective solutions based on close coordination and solidarity. OECD membership will give us permanent access to the OECD data and expertise in order to design and implement effective policy solutions tailored to our national circumstances. Our experts have already the opportunity to participate in policy discussions on cutting-edge issues and bring to the table Romania’s experiences in all areas of public policy. Given the OECD’s role in global governance through the G7 and G20, OECD membership will also enable Romania to have a voice in shaping global debate beyond Europe. Thus, the accession to the OECD helps us not only to strengthen our position in the international community, but also to reinforce our commitment to fundamental values and sustainable prosperity. In Romania, there has been a conceptual evolution of good governance in general, but OECD gives us a new perspective – a shift from public administration to public management and to public governance. Improving public governance is not just an activity of filling the gap between people’s expectations of public service and reality. It is also a challenging process, based on mutual trust between members of the society, to identify an improved relationship between government, business environment and civil society. This is done through interaction at individual, organizational, regional and national levels, in order to create a dynamic society. As part of the accession process to the OECD, we want to build a culture of solid, value-based public governance, being aware that this is an ongoing and challenging process of shaping organizational and individual practices and behaviour. I can assure you that, thanks to the OECD, concrete steps are being taken in the public sector towards more value-based performance. This is the path to modernization, which we are committed to follow. Nine O’Clock : Where has Romania made progress in governance reforms, and where does improvement remain necessary? Luca Niculescu : : Romania has made significant strides in governance reforms, in different areas, and let me give you some concrete examples on that: Centre of Government Coordination : Recent reforms have focused on strengthening the coordination function of the Romania’s Centre of Government, comprising entities like the General Secretariat of the Government and the Prime Minister’s Chancellery, particularly in terms of strategic planning and regulatory quality. Anti-bribery : One milestone in the accession process is Romania’s accession to the Convention on Combating Bribery of Foreign Public Officials in International Business Transactions (known as the OECD Anti-Bribery Convention). The Convention establishes legally binding standards to criminalise bribery of foreign public officials in international business transactions. It entered into force for Romania on 22 September 2023. Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) Implementation : Romania has adopted the National Strategy for the Sustainable Development of Romania 2030 (ROSDS) and adhered to the OECD Recommendation on Policy Coherence for Sustainable Development. Sectoral plans and programs reinforce efforts to implement SDGs and enhance policy coherence for sustainable development. Public Sector Innovation: Romania has established an innovation lab at the Centre of the Government and is developing its first Public Sector Innovation Strategy. Collaboration with the OECD Observatory of Public Sector Innovation (OPSI) aims to assess and strengthen the public sector’s innovative capacity. Gender Equality and Youth Empowerment: Romania is advancing gender equality through institutions like the National Agency for Equal Opportunities for Women and Men (ANES) and the development of Gender Equality Plans. Efforts to empower youth include adapting the strategic framework to EU Youth Strategy and offering Official Internship Programmes in the public administration. Open Government: Romania’s efforts to promote open government are aligned with the OECD standards and practices. The country is in the process of adopting its first National Strategy for Open Governance, aiming to increase public consultation and stakeholder involvement in policymaking. Digital Government: Romania is transitioning from e-Government to Digital Government, focusing on using digital technologies to transform public sector operations and service delivery. Initiatives like Digital Identity Management and the Strategic Roadmap for the Digital Decade 2030 facilitate this transformation. Public Employment and Management Systems: Romania is modernizing its public administration by implementing modern principles of human resource management. Initiatives by agencies like the National Agency of Civil Servants (NACS) and the National Administration Institute (INA) focus on digital transformation, competency frameworks, and training. Public Procurement: Romania has defined key functions of public procurement policy management, developed a National Strategy in the field of Public Procurement and continues addressing integrity risks through dedicated projects financed by the EU with OECD consultancy. Further efforts should be for example invested in capacity building for digital government initiatives; enhancing stakeholder engagement and transparency in open government practices; ensuring effective implementation of gender equality and youth empowerment strategies; addressing integrity risks in public procurement, and continuing the modernization of public administration. By focusing on these areas, we can further strengthen our governance framework and promote transparency, accountability, and efficiency in the public administration. Nine O’Clock : : Was the establishment of AMEPIP a mandatory condition for Romania from the OECD to fulfil? Luca Niculescu: The Agency for Monitoring and Assessing the Performance of State-owned Enterprises (AMEPIP) has been created considering both horizontal reforms aimed at increasing the resilience of all state-owned enterprises in line with the OECD principles on corporate governance, as well as sectoral reforms undertaken within the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (NRRP). In 2023, the regulatory state-owned enterprises framework was amended, with the support of the OECD and the European Commission. Therefore, the establishment of AMEPIP was an important step to ensure the efficiency and effectiveness of public companies. We are specifically talking about the effective administration and management of public enterprises as one of the essential elements of corporate governance. Setting-up clear objectives for public companies and ensuring transparency and professionalism in the Management Board selection process, create the premises for an efficient administration and management of public enterprises in Romania. Exclusive statement for Nine O’Clock Luca Niculescu: Further to joining NATO and the EU, OECD accession is a strategic cross-party priority for Romania, as it represents a third anchor in the community of like-minded states sharing common values, believing in the principles of a transparent and open market economy and promoting effective multilateralism in a rules-based international order. OECD membership will help improve public policies of high interest to citizens and stakeholders, as well as allow us to actively engage in debates on forward-oriented topics, such as taxation in a climate-mitigation approach, artificial intelligence, technologies of the future. We will have the opportunity to directly contribute to the joint development of global rules and systems. As a think-tank and a do-tank, OECD offers a platform for continuous testing of public policies against the best international standards through an evidence-based approach, to the benefit of all citizens. Romania remains committed to use the accession process as an opportunity and a catalyst for continued internal reform and for modernizing the public administration. We own the reforms and fully make use of the transformative capacity of the OECD.
